'''Joseph Heitman''' is an American physician-scientist focused on research in genetics, microbiology, and infectious diseases. He is the [[James B. Duke Professor]] and Chair of the Department of Molecular Genetics and Microbiology at [[Duke University School of Medicine]].<ref name=fac>{{cite web|url=https://mgm.duke.edu/faculty-and-research/primary-faculty/joseph-heitman-md-phd-2/ |access-date=23 July 2019 |title=Joseph Heitman, MD, PhD |publisher=Duke University School of Medicine}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Joseph Heitman grew up in southwestern [[Michigan]] and attended [[Portage Northern High School]].<ref name=JCI2>{{cite journal|doi=10.1172/jci.insight.99816|pmid=29467327|pmc=5916239|title=Talking TOR: A conversation with Joe Heitman and Rao Movva|journal=JCI Insight|volume=3|issue=4|year=2018|last1=Williams|first1=Corinne L. |article-number=e99816 }}</ref> He completed a dual [[Bachelor of Science]]–[[Master of Science]] program in chemistry and biochemistry at the [[University of Chicago]] from 1980 to 1984.<ref name=facbio>{{cite web|url=https://mgm.duke.edu/faculty-and-research/primary-faculty/joseph-heitman-md-phd-2/joseph-heitman-md-phd-biography/ |access-date=23 July 2019 |title=Joseph Heitman, MD, PhD - Biography |publisher=Duke University School of Medicine}}</ref> There he began his research career, working in the laboratories of organic chemist [[Josef Fried]], biochemist [[Kan Agarwal]], and bacteriologist [[Malcolm Casadaban]].<ref name=JCI2/><ref name=JCI>{{cite journal|doi=10.1172/JCI120588|pmid=29608142|pmc=5873853|title=Joseph Heitman receives the 2018 ASCI/Korsmeyer Award|journal=Journal of Clinical Investigation|volume=128|issue=4|pages=1205–1207|year=2018|last1=Jackson|first1=Sarah}}</ref> In 1984, he began a dual [[MD–PhD]] program at [[Cornell Medical College]] and [[Rockefeller University]], working on [[DNA repair]] in bacteria with [[Peter Model]] and [[Norton Zinder]].<ref name=facbio/> In 1989, after receiving his PhD from Rockefeller University, Heitman took a leave of absence from medical school to serve as an [[European Molecular Biology Organization|EMBO]]-sponsored long-term fellow at the [[Biozentrum University of Basel]] working with [[Michael N. Hall]] and [[Rao Movva]] applying yeast genetics to understand the mechanisms of action of immunosuppressive drugs.<ref name=facbio/><ref name=plos>{{cite journal|doi=10.1371/journal.ppat.1005245|pmid=26540102|pmc=4634758|title=On the Discovery of TOR as the Target of Rapamycin|journal=PLOS Pathogens|volume=11|issue=11|article-number=e1005245|year=2015|last1=Heitman|first1=Joseph |doi-access=free }}</ref> This work led to the discovery of the cellular growth regulator [[mTOR|TOR]] for which Michael Hall was awarded the [[Albert Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research]] in 2017.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.laskerfoundation.org/awards/show/nutrient-activated-tor-proteins-regulate-cell-growth/#overview |access-date=23 July 2019 |title=2017 Lasker Awards |publisher=Albert and Mary Lasker Foundation}}</ref><ref name="Science">{{cite journal | vauthors = Heitman J, Movva NR, Hall MN | title = Targets for cell cycle arrest by the immunosuppressant rapamycin in yeast | journal = Science | volume = 253 | issue = 5022 | pages = 905–9 | date = August 1991 | pmid = 1715094 | doi = 10.1126/science.1715094| bibcode = 1991Sci...253..905H | s2cid = 9937225 }}</ref> In 1992, Heitman finished medical school and moved to Duke University to set up his own laboratory in the Department of Molecular Genetics and Microbiology.<ref name=facbio/><ref name=JCI/> He was an investigator with the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] from 1992 to 2005 and a Burroughs Wellcome Scholar in Molecular Pathogenic Mycology from 1998 to 2005.<ref name=HHMI>{{cite web|url=https://www.hhmi.org/scientists/joseph-heitman|access-date=23 May 2020 |title=Joseph Heitman, MD, PhD HHMI alumnus investigator |publisher=Howard Hughes Medical Institute}}</ref> He became Chair of the Department of Molecular Genetics and Microbiology in 2009.<ref name=facbio/> Since 2019, Heitman has been co-director of the [[Canadian Institute for Advanced Research]]'s Fungal Kingdom program along with co-director [[Leah E. Cowen]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://medschool.duke.edu/about-us/news-and-communications/med-school-blog/heitman-and-cowen-awarded-cifar-research-program-fungal-kingdom-threats-opportunities |access-date=12 September 2019 |publisher=Duke University Medical School |date=8 April 2019 |title=Heitman and Cowen Awarded CIFAR for Research Program "The Fungal Kingdom: Threats & Opportunities" |archive-date=27 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190927012737/https://medschool.duke.edu/about-us/news-and-communications/med-school-blog/heitman-and-cowen-awarded-cifar-research-program-fungal-kingdom-threats-opportunities }}</ref>

Heitman's research has been recognized with prestigious awards and funding opportunities, including funding by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute from 1992 to 2005, and an [[National Institutes of Health MERIT Award]] from 2011-2021.<ref name=HHMI/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://corporate.dukehealth.org/news-listing/duke-physician-scientist-receives-prestigious-nih-merit-award-studies-fungal-unisexual |access-date=23 May 2020 |publisher=Duke Health |title=duke-physician-scientist-receives-prestigious-nih-merit-award-studies-fungal-unisexual|date=21 June 2011 }}</ref> Several awards have recognized his research accomplishments, including the 
ASBMB AMGEN Award (2002), the IDSA Squibb Award (2003) (now called the [[Oswald Avery]] Award), the [[Stanley J. Korsmeyer Award]] (2018) (for key contributions to understanding how microbial pathogens evolve, cause disease, and develop drug resistance and discovery of TOR and FKBP12 as targets of rapamycin), the Rhoda Benham Award (2018), the [[Edward Novitski Prize]] (2019) (honoring work on human fungal pathogens and identifying molecular targets of widely used immunosuppressive drugs, a seminal contribution to discovery of TOR, which regulates cell growth in response to nutrients), the [[American Society for Microbiology]]'s Award for Basic Research (2019), and the Distinguished Mycologist Award from the [[Mycological Society of America]] (2021).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://corporate.dukehealth.org/news/duke-molecular-biologist-receives-commendation |access-date=2 October 2020 |publisher=Duke University News |title=Molecular Biologist Receives Commendation|date=27 August 2001 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.idsociety.org/about-idsa/awards/oswald-avery-award-winners/ |access-date=2 October 2020 |publisher=Infectious Diseases Society of America |title=IDSA Award Recipients}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.the-asci.org/awards/korsmeyer |access-date=12 September 2019 |publisher=American Society for Clinical Investigation |title=Stanley J. Korsmeyer Award |archive-date=13 June 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170613015801/https://www.the-asci.org/award/ }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mycologicalsociety.org/rhoda_benham_awardees |access-date=2 October 2020 |publisher=Medical Mycological Society of America |title=Rhoda Benham Award Recipients |work=Medical ==Research==
Heitman's research has largely focused on studies of model and pathogenic fungi to address unsolved problems in biology and medicine. Pioneering research with the model budding yeast ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' discovered TOR and FKBP12 as the targets of the immunosuppressive and antiproliferative drug rapamycin, now widely used in organ transplantation and cancer chemotherapy.<ref name="Cloning and deletion of the yeast gene encoding FKBP12">{{cite journal | vauthors = Heitman, J, Movva, NR, Hiestand, PC, Hall, MN | title = FK506-binding protein proline rotamase is a target for the immunosuppressive agent FK506 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae | journal = Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A | volume = 88 | issue = 5 | pages = 1948–1952 | date = March 1991 | pmid = 1705713 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.88.5.1948| pmc = 51143 | bibcode = 1991PNAS...88.1948H | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="Discovery of FKBP12 and TOR as the target of rapamycin">{{cite journal | vauthors = Heitman, J, Movva, NR, Hall, MN | title = Targets for cell cycle arrest by the immunosuppressant rapamycin in yeast | journal = Science | volume = 253 | issue = 5022 | pages = 905–909 | date = August 23, 1991 | pmid = 1715094 | doi = 10.1126/science.1715094| bibcode = 1991Sci...253..905H | s2cid = 9937225 }}</ref>  Later studies elucidated key features of how the TOR signaling pathway senses nutrients to control cellular responses.<ref name="TOR pathway senses nutrients to control gene expression programs">{{cite journal |vauthors=Cardenas ME, Cutler NS, Lorenz MC, Di Como CJ, Heitman J | title = The TOR signaling cascade regulates gene expression in response to nutrients| journal = Genes Dev | volume = 13 | issue = 24 | pages = 3271–3279 | date = December 1999 | pmid = 10617575 | doi = 10.1101/gad.13.24.3271| pmc = 317202| doi-access = free }}</ref> Studies were conducted on the dimorphic transition of ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' from budding yeast cells to pseudohyphae, elucidating nutrient sensing signaling cascades governing this morphological transition involving GPCR-cAMP-PKA signaling cascades controlling gene expression, and discovering a novel role for the ammonium permease/Rh antigen homolog Mep2 as a transceptor for nitrogen source availability.<ref name="Gpa2 and yeast PHG">{{cite journal | vauthors = Lorenz, MC, Heitman, J | title = Yeast pseudohyphal growth is regulated by GPA2, a G protein alpha homolog | journal = EMBO Journal | volume = 16 | issue = 23 | pages = 7008–7018 | date = December 1997 | pmid = 9384580 | pmc = 1170304 | doi = 10.1093/emboj/16.23.7008}}</ref><ref name="Mep2 and yeast PHG">{{cite journal | vauthors = Lorenz, MC, Heitman, J | title = The MEP2 ammonium permease regulates pseudohyphal differentiation in ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' | journal = EMBO Journal | volume = 17 | issue = 5 | pages = 1236–1247 | date = August 1998 | pmid = 9482721 | pmc = 1170472 | doi = 10.1093/emboj/17.5.1236}}</ref><ref name="Gpr1 GPCR and yeast PHG">{{cite journal | vauthors = Lorenz, MC, Pan, X, Harashima, T, Cardenas, ME, Xue, Y, Hirsch, JP, Heitman, J | title = The G protein-coupled receptor Gpr1 is a nutrient sensor that regulates pseudohyphal differentiation in ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' | journal = Genetics | volume = 154 | issue = 2 | pages = 609–622 | date = February 2000 | doi = 10.1093/genetics/154.2.609 | pmid = 10655215 | pmc = 1460933 }}</ref><ref name="PKA catalytic subunits play specialized roles in yeast PHG">{{cite journal | vauthors = Pan, X, Heitman, J | title = Cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase regulates pseudohyphal differentiation in ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' | journal = Mol Cell Biol | volume = 19 | issue = 7 | pages = 4874–4887 | date = July 1999 | pmid = 10373537 | pmc = 84286 | doi = 10.1128/mcb.19.7.4874}}</ref><ref name="PKA molecular switch">{{cite journal | vauthors = Pan, X, Heitman, J | title = Protein kinase A operates a molecular switch that governs yeast pseudohyphal differentiation | journal = Mol Cell Biol | volume = 22 | issue = 12 | pages = 3981–3993 | date = June 2002 | pmid = 12024012 | pmc = 133872 | doi = 10.1128/mcb.22.12.3981-3993.2002}}</ref><ref name="Yeast PHG review">{{cite journal | vauthors = Pan, X, Harashima, T, Heitman, J | title = Signal transduction cascades regulating pseudohyphal differentiation of ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' | journal = Curr Opin Microbiol | volume = 3 | issue = 6 | pages = 567–572 | date = December 2000 | pmid = 11121775 | doi = 10.1016/s1369-5274(00)00142-9}}</ref><ref name="Fungal signal transduction review">{{cite journal | vauthors = Lengeler, KB, Davidson, RC, D'souza, C, Harashima, T, Shen, WC, Wang, P, Pan, X, Waugh, M, Heitman, J | title = Signal transduction cascades regulating fungal development and virulence | journal = Microbiol Mol Biol Rev | volume = 64 | issue = 4 | pages = 746–785 | date = December 2000 | pmid = 11104818 | pmc = 99013 | doi = 10.1128/mmbr.64.4.746-785.2000}}</ref>
 
Heitman's research program has also focused extensive studies on the pathogenesis, sexual cycle, and novel drug targets of the pathogenic fungus ''[[Cryptococcus]]''.<ref name=facbio/> His group described a previously unknown form of sexual reproduction in ''Cryptococcus'' species, known as unisexual reproduction, which involves both selfing sexual reproduction (homothallism) of isolates grown on their own without a mating partner, as well as sexual reproduction and recombination involving cell-cell fusion between individuals of the same mating type followed by meiosis and sporulation.<ref name="NatureA">{{cite journal | vauthors = Lin, X, Hull, CM, Heitman J | title = Sexual reproduction between partners of the same mating type in Cryptococcus neoformans | journal = Nature | volume = 434 | issue = 7036 | pages = 1017–21 | date = April 2005 | pmid = 15846346 | doi = 10.1038/nature03448| bibcode = 2005Natur.434.1017L | s2cid = 52857557 }}</ref><ref name=gsa>{{cite web|url=http://genestogenomes.org/2019-edward-novitski-prize-awarded-to-joseph-heitman/ |access-date=23 July 2019 |title=2019 Edward Novitski Prize awarded to Joseph Heitman |date=12 February 2019 |publisher=Genetics Society of America}}</ref> Studies conducted in parallel defined and illuminated evolution and function of fungal mating-type loci, illustrating parallels with sex chromosome evolution of plants and animals, including the discovery and characterization of the homeodomain proteins Sxi1alpha and Sxi2a, which coordinately control cell type identity and sexual reproduction.<ref name="MAT locus cloning">{{cite journal |vauthors=Lengeler KB, Fox DS, Fraser JA, Allen A, Forrester K, Dietrich FS, Heitman J | title = Mating-type locus of Cryptococcus neoformans: a step in the evolution of sex chromosomes | journal = Eukaryotic Cell | volume = 1 | issue = 5 | pages = 704–718 | date = October 2002 | pmid = 12455690 | doi = 10.1128/ec.1.5.704-718.2002 | pmc = 126754 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="MAT locus comparative genomics">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fraser, JA, Diezmann, S, Subaran, RL, Allen, A, Lengeler, KB, Dietrich, FS, Heitman, J | title = Convergent evolution of chromosomal sex-determining regions in the animal and fungal kingdoms | journal = PLOS Biology | volume = 2 | issue = 12 | article-number = e384 | date = December 2004 | pmid = 15538538 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pbio.0020384 | pmc = 526376 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="MAT review 1">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fraser, JA, Heitman, J | title = Evolution of fungal sex chromosomes | journal = Molecular Microbiology | volume = 51 | issue = 2 | pages = 299–306 | date = January 2004 | pmid = 14756773 | doi = 10.1046/j.1365-2958.2003.03874.x | s2cid = 2467616 }}</ref><ref name="MAT review 2">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fraser, JA, Heitman, J | title = Chromosomal sex-determining regions in animals, plants and fungi | journal = Curr Opin Genet Dev | volume = 15 | issue = 6 | pages = 645–651 | date = September 2005 | pmid = 16182521 | doi = 10.1016/j.gde.2005.09.002}}</ref><ref name="Sxi1">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hull, CM, Davidson, RC, Heitman, J | title = Cell identity and sexual development in Cryptococcus neoformans are controlled by the mating-type-specific homeodomain protein Sxi1alpha | journal = Genes Dev | volume = 16 | issue = 23 | pages = 3046–3060 | date = December 2002 | pmid = 12464634 | doi = 10.1101/gad.1041402 | pmc = 187491 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="Sxi2">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hull, CM, Boily, MJ, Heitman, J | title = Sex-specific homeodomain proteins Sxi1alpha and Sxi2a coordinately regulate sexual development in Cryptococcus neoformans | journal = Eukaryotic Cell | volume = 4 | issue = 3 | pages = 526–535 | date = March 2005 | pmid = 15755915 | doi = 10.1128/EC.4.3.526-535.2005 | pmc = 1087792 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
Heitman's group has also had a long-standing interest in fungal evolution, describing how cellular processes such as sexual recombination and [[RNA interference]] are changed in different fungal lineages, as well as the expansion of the geographic range of the emerging pathogen ''[[Cryptococcus gattii]]''.<ref name=facbio/><ref name=gsa/><ref name="NatureB">{{cite journal | vauthors = Calo S, Shertz-Wall C, Lee SC, Bastidas RJ, Nicolás FE, Granek JA, Mieczkowski P, Torres-Martínez S, Ruiz-Vázquez RM, Cardenas ME, Heitman J | title = Antifungal drug resistance evoked via RNAi-dependent ==Roles as editor and in scientific publishing==
